# Host package upgrades (`bay host upgrade`)

`bay host upgrade <env> --box <box>` upgrades the OS packages of one box. It runs
`apt-get dist-upgrade`, finishes dpkg, repairs the firewall when the upgrade
flushed it, reboots on request, and checks the box. It replaces the manual
`systemd-run apt-get dist-upgrade` and reboot.

## Why a command

A manual upgrade had three problems:

- It collided with a running `bay up`. apt held the dpkg lock, the deploy died
  on it, and a project was left half deployed.
- Nothing told the operator that a reboot was pending. Boxes ran for more than
  200 days on an old kernel.
- An upgrade of the `nftables` package flushed the whole firewall (see
  [The firewall after an upgrade](#the-firewall-after-an-upgrade)).

## Usage

```bash
bay host upgrade production --box alpha                     # upgrade, check
bay host upgrade production --box alpha --reboot            # also reboot when needed
bay host upgrade production --box alpha -- --check          # dry run: list packages, change nothing
bay host upgrade production --box alpha --json --log /tmp/upgrade.log
```

- `--box` is required. The command runs on exactly one box. It never runs on
  the whole environment. Upgrade `alpha`, check it, then upgrade `beta`.
- The box must be in `bay.fleet.toml` with `env = "<env>"`, and it must map to
  exactly one inventory host. A box whose group holds two hosts is refused.
- When two boxes share one host, the command upgrades the host. The result
  names the other box in `boxes_on_host`.
- The fleet is checked first, as for `bay deploy`: it is fetched, a fleet that
  is only behind is pulled, and a dirty or diverged fleet is refused
  (`--offline`, `--allow-dirty`, `--allow-older-bay`).
- Arguments after `--` go to `ansible-playbook`. `-l`, `--limit`, `--tags` and
  `--skip-tags` are refused: the command picks the host, and the role runs
  whole.
- The command writes no deploy receipt and no lock record. The fleet does not
  change.

## What it does on the box

1. It refuses a busy box (see [The deploy lock](#the-deploy-lock)).
2. It takes the deploy lock.
3. It records the running kernel, the running containers and the start time of
   `nftables.service`.
4. It runs `apt-get update`, then lists the packages with
   `apt-get -s dist-upgrade`.
5. It starts `apt-get -y dist-upgrade` in a transient systemd unit,
   `bay-host-upgrade`, with `--force-confdef --force-confold`. Changed
   config files keep their local version. The output goes to
   `/var/log/bay-host-upgrade.log`, the exit code to
   `/var/lib/bay/host-upgrade/rc`. apt waits up to 10 minutes for a dpkg lock
   that another process holds, such as unattended-upgrades.
6. It polls the exit code. The unit runs outside the SSH session, so an
   upgrade of tailscale or openssh can drop the session and apt goes on. A
   dropped session ends one poll round; the next round waits for the
   connection again. The run fails after `host_upgrade_timeout` (2400 s).
7. When apt exits with an error, it runs one repair pass (see
   [When apt fails](#when-apt-fails)).
8. It runs `dpkg --configure -a`, then `dpkg --audit`.
9. It repairs the firewall when needed
   (see [The firewall after an upgrade](#the-firewall-after-an-upgrade)).
10. It decides if a reboot is needed: `/var/run/reboot-required` exists, or the
    newest kernel in `/lib/modules` is not the running one. With `--reboot` it
    reboots and waits for the box. Without `--reboot` it says that a reboot is
    pending. It never reboots when the apt step failed.
11. It runs the checks, releases the lock and writes the result.

## When apt fails

A known race: the postinst of `crowdsec-firewall-bouncer-nftables` starts the
bouncer while CrowdSec restarts. The bouncer cannot reach the CrowdSec API, the
start fails, and `apt-get dist-upgrade` exits 100. The package stays half
configured. A live trial hit this on a real upgrade of 78 packages.

So a failed first pass does not end the run. The command runs one repair pass:

1. When CrowdSec is installed, it waits until `cscli lapi status` answers, up
   to `host_upgrade_crowdsec_wait` (60 s). It goes on after that time also.
2. It runs `dpkg --configure -a`.
3. It runs `apt-get -f install -y` and then one more `dist-upgrade`, with the
   same flags. These run in the same detached unit, and they append to the
   same log.

The apt step fails only when the repair pass fails, or when `dpkg --audit`
still lists a package. The result says `apt_repair: true` and gives the exit
code of the first pass in `apt_first_rc`.

When the apt step fails after the unit started, the run still does the rest:

- It repairs the firewall and runs every check. The result always has
  `checks` and `containers.after`.
- It does not reboot, also with `--reboot`. A half configured kernel or
  initramfs can stop the box from booting. `reboot_note` says why.
- It releases the deploy lock.
- Then it fails, and `failed_task` names the apt step
  (`Fail when apt-get failed`).

When the unit does not end in time, apt still runs. Then the command does not
touch the firewall, because a Docker restart in the middle of dpkg can break a
package. It runs the checks and fails.

## The firewall after an upgrade

`nftables.service` has `ExecStop=nft flush ruleset`. An upgrade of the
`nftables` package stops and starts the unit. The stop flushes the whole
ruleset: the Bay tables, Docker's NAT and filter rules, and the CrowdSec sets.
The start loads only `/etc/nftables.conf`. Docker writes its rules only when it
starts. So published ports and container egress stay broken until Docker
restarts. On a real box this lasted 49 seconds, and only because the Docker
package was in the same upgrade.

The command repairs the firewall when one of these is true:

- the `nftables` package was in the upgrade,
- `nftables.service` started again during the run,
- a Docker chain is missing (`iptables -t nat -L DOCKER`,
  `iptables -t filter -L DOCKER`).

The repair has a fixed order:

1. `nft -f /etc/nftables.conf`. This file includes `/etc/nftables.d/*.conf`,
   so the egress and pre-routing tables return.
2. `systemctl restart docker`. Docker writes its rules on top of the loaded
   firewall. Containers with a restart policy start again.
3. `systemctl restart crowdsec-firewall-bouncer`, so its sets return.

Then the checks wait for the containers. The result says `firewall.repaired`
and why.

## The checks

Every check has a name. A failed check fails the run with its name. When the
apt step failed too, the run names the apt step, and the checks are in the
result.

| Check | Passes when |
|-------|-------------|
| `docker` | `docker.service` is active and `docker info` answers. |
| `containers` | Every container that ran before runs again. A container with a healthcheck must be healthy. The check waits up to `host_upgrade_container_wait` (300 s). |
| `container_restarts` | No container that ran before is in state `restarting`, and no restart count grew between the start of the wait and `host_upgrade_restart_window` (30 s) after the containers are back. A failure names the container and prints its last 20 log lines. A container in a loop can look `Up` at one sample, so the count is the stronger sign. |
| `nftables` | `nftables.service` is active. Only where the unit exists. |
| `nftables_tables` | `table inet filter` is loaded. Also `table inet bay_prerouting` when `/etc/nftables.d/bay-prerouting.conf` exists, and `table inet bay_egress` and `table bridge bay_egress` when `/etc/nftables.d/bay-egress.conf` exists. |
| `docker_chains` | Docker's `DOCKER` chains exist in the `nat` and `filter` tables. |
| `published_port` | The lowest TCP port that a container publishes on `0.0.0.0` or `127.0.0.1` answers on `127.0.0.1`. Only when a container publishes one. This check is weaker than `docker_chains`: a local connection can go through `docker-proxy`. |
| `crowdsec`, `crowdsec_bouncer` | The unit is active. Only where the unit exists. |
| `tailscale` | `tailscaled` is active, its `BackendState` is `Running`, and `tailscale ip -4` gives an address. Only where the unit exists. |

The kernel before and after is in the result. It is not a check.

Why the restart check: after a cold boot, Traefik runs with the host network
and binds a tailnet address. It started before tailscaled had that address,
failed to bind, and restarted in a loop. Every site of the box was down while
`docker ps` showed Traefik as `Up` between two restarts. The sysctl
`net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1` from the traefik role fixes the loop itself
(2.18.1). The check makes such a loop fail the run instead of passing it.

## The deploy lock

The upgrade uses the same lock file as a deploy: `<stack_dir>/.deploy.lock`
(`deploy_lock_path`). The file holds `"kind": "host_upgrade"`.

Before it starts, the upgrade refuses when:

- the fleet holds a fresh claim of a `bay up` on the box env (`env_busy`,
  exit 43). This is the same claim that stops a second `bay up`
  ([plan.md](plan.md)). A claim older than 30 minutes, or one that this
  machine can prove dead, does not count. A `bay up` for one project deploys
  only the boxes it needs, but its claim names the box env. So the upgrade
  waits for any `bay up` on that box env, whichever box the run touches.
- the box holds the deploy lock and the lock is younger than
  `deploy_lock_timeout` (3600 s) (`box_locked`, exit 43).
- the unit `bay-host-upgrade` still runs from an earlier upgrade
  (`upgrade_running`, exit 43).

While the upgrade runs, a deploy stops:

- `deploy.yml` and `provision.yml` start with a guard
  (`roles/host_upgrade/tasks/guard.yml`). It stops the run before any role
  touches the box, when the lock holds `"kind": "host_upgrade"` and is fresh,
  or when the unit `bay-host-upgrade` is active. The message says that a host
  upgrade runs and names its log.
- `deploy_stack` still checks the lock as before, and its message now says
  when a host upgrade holds it.

How the lock is released:

- The upgrade removes the lock at the end, also when it fails.
- The upgrade touches the lock at the start of each poll round, so a long
  upgrade keeps it fresh.
- When the controller dies (Ctrl-C, a crash, a lost connection), nobody
  removes or touches the lock. It goes stale after `deploy_lock_timeout`, and
  then a deploy and an upgrade ignore it. While the apt unit still runs, the
  guard refuses a deploy anyway, because it also checks the unit.
- To clear a lock that you know is dead, remove `<stack_dir>/.deploy.lock` on
  the box.

The check of the lock and the write of the lock are two steps, as in
`deploy_stack`. Two runs that start in the same second can both pass the check.

## Dry run

`bay host upgrade <env> --box <box> -- --check` changes nothing on the box. It
writes no lock, runs no apt, restarts nothing and does not reboot. It lists the
packages that a real run would upgrade, against the package lists that are
already on the box, and runs the checks against the box as it is.
`packages_upgraded` is 0 and `dry_run` is true.

## The JSON result

`--json` prints one document on stdout. With `--log`, progress and the Ansible
output go to the log file.

With `--log` and no `--json`, the terminal shows a short summary at the end:
the result word, the key facts (packages upgraded, a repair pass, a pending or
done reboot, every check), the PLAY RECAP counts per host (ok, changed,
failed) and the log path. `bay deploy` and `bay provision` with `--log` end
with the same summary, without the upgrade facts.

```json
{
  "result_version": 1,
  "ok": true,
  "env": "production",
  "box": "alpha",
  "host": "alpha.example.com",
  "boxes_on_host": ["alpha"],
  "dry_run": false,
  "reason": null,
  "error": null,
  "failed_task": null,
  "box_touched": true,
  "packages_upgraded": 2,
  "packages": ["docker-ce", "tailscale"],
  "apt_first_rc": 100,
  "apt_repair": true,
  "apt_rc": 0,
  "dpkg_audit": [],
  "reboot_required": true,
  "rebooted": false,
  "reboot_note": null,
  "kernel": {"before": "6.1.0-25-amd64", "after": "6.1.0-25-amd64", "newest_installed": "6.1.0-26-amd64"},
  "containers": {"before": ["api", "postgres"], "after": ["api", "postgres"], "missing": [], "unhealthy": [],
                 "restart_loop": [], "restart_counts": {"api": 0, "postgres": 0}, "logs": {}},
  "firewall": {"repaired": false, "why": []},
  "checks": [{"name": "docker", "ok": true, "detail": "docker is active and answers"}],
  "log": "/var/log/bay-host-upgrade.log"
}
```

| Exit | Reason | Meaning |
|------|--------|---------|
| 0 | `null` | The upgrade ran and every check passed. |
| 43 | `env_busy` | A `bay up` holds a claim on the box env. `holder` names it. Nothing was touched. |
| 43 | `box_locked`, `upgrade_running` | The box holds the deploy lock, or an upgrade unit still runs. Nothing was changed. |
| 41, 42, 45 | as `bay deploy` | The fleet is not in sync, the push was refused, or the Bay version is too old. |
| 1 | `failed` | apt failed, the unit did not end in time, or a check failed. `failed_task` and `error` say which. |

The apt fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `apt_first_rc` | The exit code of the first `dist-upgrade` pass. `null` when apt did not run. |
| `apt_repair` | `true` when the first pass failed and the repair pass ran. |
| `apt_rc` | The exit code of the last pass. |
| `dpkg_audit` | The lines of `dpkg --audit`. Empty when every package is configured. |
| `reboot_note` | Why the box was not rebooted with `--reboot`, or `null`. |

## Settings

Set these in `group_vars` to change the defaults
(`roles/host_upgrade/defaults/main.yml`):

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `host_upgrade_timeout` | `2400` | Seconds the poll waits for the apt unit. Keep it below `deploy_lock_timeout`. |
| `host_upgrade_container_wait` | `300` | Seconds the checks wait for the containers. |
| `host_upgrade_restart_window` | `30` | Seconds the checks watch the containers for a restart loop after they are back. |
| `host_upgrade_log_lines` | `20` | Log lines printed for a container in a restart loop. |
| `host_upgrade_reboot_timeout` | `900` | Seconds to wait for the box after a reboot. |
| `host_upgrade_dpkg_lock_timeout` | `600` | Seconds apt waits for a dpkg lock that another process holds. |
| `host_upgrade_crowdsec_wait` | `60` | Seconds the repair pass waits for `cscli lapi status` to answer. |
| `host_upgrade_docker_chains` | `nat/DOCKER`, `filter/DOCKER` | The Docker chains the repair and the check look for. |

## Not tested without a real box

The tests run the role on the test machine with fake commands. These steps
need a live trial on a test box:

- a real `apt-get dist-upgrade` in the transient unit, and the rc file;
- a dropped SSH session during the poll (a tailscale upgrade), and the next
  round that reconnects;
- the reboot with `ansible.builtin.reboot` and the checks after it, with a
  real restart loop and a real `tailscale ip -4` right after the boot;
- the real flush by the nftables package, the reload, and Docker writing its
  rules again;
- the repair pass after the CrowdSec bouncer race: the wait for
  `cscli lapi status`, `apt-get -f install` and the second `dist-upgrade`;
- a `bay up` or `bay deploy` started during the upgrade, which must stop at
  the guard.
